query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a coating or surface modification with a corrosion-resistant layer, such as a high-entropy alloy or a ceramic layer, to boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment
generation.intervention: Coating or surface modification with a corrosion-resistant layer
generation.mechanism: The corrosion-resistant layer acts as a barrier against molten aluminum, reducing the contact between the boride-based component and the corrosive environment, thus improving the component's resistance to corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion, potentially leading to increased service life and reduced maintenance costs
generation.baseline: Untreated boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the coating or surface modification may depend on factors such as the type and thickness of the corrosion-resistant layer, the surface preparation of the boride-based component, and the specific conditions of the hot-dip aluminum-plating environment
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in corrosion resistance and the optimal characteristics of the corrosion-resistant layer are uncertain and require further research

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled experiment comparing the corrosion resistance of untreated boride-based components with those coated or surface-modified with a corrosion-resistant layer in a hot-dip aluminum-plating environment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated or surface-modified components show no significant improvement in corrosion resistance compared to the untreated components, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The effects of alloying with zirconium on the microstructure, elastic modulus, and corrosion properties of a high-entropy alloy, from the CoCrFeNiMo system, were investigated. A simulated corrosive solution (3.5% NaCl) was used to characterize the corrosion behavior of these materials using electrochemical techniques. A brittle fracture with a cleavage-like fracture plane could be observed for both alloys. The alloy without zirconium was more resistant to corrosion, with a very low corrosion rate (2.44 × 10−3 mmpy in comparison with 2.80 × 10−3 mmpy for the sample with Zr). The resistance of the passive film decreased with the addition of Zr (from 2.57 × 107 kΩ·cm2 to 1.47 × 105 kΩ·cm2) due to the increased number of defects points in the film. Doping with 0.71 wt.% Zr produced grain refinement and increased the hardness but did not increase the modulus of elasticity or corrosion resistance of the CoCrFeNiMo alloy.

In this work, a reinforced layer on the surface of HEA was successfully synthesized by powder-pack boriding. The microstructure, microhardness, wear resistance, and boriding mechanism were investigated. The following conclusions can be summarized: The microstructure of the surface layer is mainly composed of MB-type boride and M2B-type boride. The original interface of the surface layer is located at the interface between the BL and the diffusion layer, where element B diffuses inward and metal elements diffuse outward. The activation energy and frequency factor of the B element in CoCrFeMnNi HEA are 206.93 kJ/mol and 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s, respectively. Increasing the boronizing duration and temperature resulted in an increase in the BL and diffusion layer thickness. The surface strengthening of CoCrFeMnNi HEA was achieved by the boriding treatment. Its surface microhardness has significantly increased from 3.9 ± 0.1 Gpa to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa. The surface layer shows a lower friction coefficient of 0.48 than that of the substrate (0.86). ZrC can effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating, and the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating increases with increasing ZrC content. The annual corrosion rate of the 04ZrC coating in a 1 mol/L NaCl solution is only 21.5% of that of the HEA. Consequently, the addition of ZrC to the FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy alloy coating holds promise for applications in corrosion resistance, particularly in oceanic environments.

In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.

decision.trend: Research has been focused on developing high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with improved corrosion resistance, particularly in extreme environments. Various studies have investigated the effects of different alloying elements, processing methods, and microstructures on the corrosion behavior of HEAs. The trend suggests that HEAs with single-phase structures, such as face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) phases, tend to exhibit better corrosion resistance than those with multiphase structures. Additionally, the incorporation of certain elements, like titanium or zirconium, has been shown to enhance corrosion resistance in some cases.
decision.unsolved: Despite the progress made in developing corrosion-resistant HEAs, there is still a need to improve their performance in specific environments, such as molten aluminum. The exact mechanisms of corrosion in these environments are not yet fully understood, and further research is required to optimize the composition and microstructure of HEAs for improved corrosion resistance.
decision.lever: coating or surface modification with a corrosion-resistant layer
decision.why: Given the trend of research focused on developing corrosion-resistant HEAs, the next plausible step would be to explore surface or interface engineering strategies to further enhance the corrosion resistance of boride-based components. Applying a coating or surface modification with a corrosion-resistant layer, such as a high-entropy alloy or a ceramic layer, could provide an additional barrier against molten aluminum corrosion. This approach could be particularly effective in combination with optimized composition and microstructure of the underlying boride-based component.
